author: haiku
reason: A keeps the runtime flow apart from the build and rollout work, uses the same Starts / What it does / Keeps its data / If it goes wrong layout for every step, collects constants and table columns in one place and ends with a failure-situation table, while B numbers build-time tasks (code refactor, migration, tests) as steps alongside the runtime flow, which blurs what actually triggers each step at runtime.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: it first describes how the existing system works, keeps the runtime flow (click, job, failure handling, page, download) apart from the build and rollout work, and has a failure table that ties each case to its step, whereas A puts build steps such as the shared module, the migration and the tests in the same numbered sequence as the runtime steps and jumps between steps (for example, from Step 6 to Step 9).

author: sonnet
reason: Document A's steps run in the order things actually happen, from click to path choice to job attempt, build, publish, email, final failure and status page, and it ends with a single table of failures; Document B puts the status page and an optional download step in the middle of the job flow, so it needs a separate map of which step belongs to which path and sends the reader back and forth between steps.

author: sonnet
reason: B is easier for an outsider to follow because it opens with the existing system and the reason the work splits into two paths, and it defines every primitive it uses (the job queue, multipart upload, the bucket and signed_url) before the steps; its steps then run in execution order, with a failure table to sum up. A puts the page-status and optional-download steps in the middle of the job flow, needs a separate map of which steps belong to which path, and sends the reader back and forth between steps (step 7 reuses sub-steps 3 to 5 of step 9).

author: haiku
reason: Document A gives a four-stage overview, numbered steps and a failure table, so a reader sees what starts each step, where state lives and what each failure does; Document B spreads the flow across nested diagram branches and a list of decisions, and adds confusing points such as window keys set by the gateway clock while Retry-After uses the Redis clock.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: it opens with a four-stage overview, walks through the request in numbered steps that say what triggers each step and where state lives (the key cache in gateway memory, the counters in Redis), and puts every failure case in one table; A spreads the same mechanism across diagram notes, design rationale and a Lua sketch.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A walks the request through numbered steps, each giving its trigger, outcome and failure, and adds a failure table, so a newcomer can follow the flow in order; Document B puts the flow mainly in the diagram and spreads the rest across topic notes (store, window, headers, fail open), which the reader has to piece together.

author: sonnet
reason: B gives a numbered prose walk-through, starting from the existing request path, with the failure case beside each step and a failure table, so a newcomer can follow what triggers each step and what happens on error without decoding A's logic, which sits mostly inside Mermaid notes.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow because it defines its core mechanisms once, as numbered steps: the guarded copy, the control-row check and the single reusable switch procedure S, with a stated commit point. A packs most of its mechanics into a long terms list, says there are three stages but then defines four lettered phases, and its phase letters collide with its sub-step letters (for example "Phase B to C" containing steps a to f).

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow because it describes how the system works today, explains the runtime write, erase and read paths, then lists the switch steps in place. A makes the reader map a generic "procedure S" with old and new sources onto each phase, and even runs it with Postgres as both old and new source, skipping steps, which adds indirection.

author: sonnet
reason: A opens with a summary of every stage, puts the runtime behaviour (writes, repair, copy rule, deletes, fence, reads, ids) in one "How the system runs" section, uses a single four-value write-mode flag that matches the stages, and ends with a failure table; B has a clean SoT/follower framing but spreads the mechanism across terms, design decisions and steps, and it uses five interacting flags (dual_write, sot, mirror and others), which make state harder to follow.

author: sonnet
reason: B opens with the current system and a roadmap of the stages, explains the runtime write, repair, read and fence behaviour in one plain-prose section, and models the migration with a single four-value write-mode flag; A spreads that same state across three interacting flags (dual_write, sot, mirror) and buries mechanism inside its glossary, so a newcomer would build the correct mental model faster from B.

author: haiku
reason: A sets out the modes, the forward gates, numbered rollback steps and a single failure table in one consistent order, while B contradicts itself on where a rollback ends ("always ends in old_only" against "the rollout returns to shadow") and labels its diagram edges with the result of the step before, which makes the order harder to follow.

author: haiku
reason: A explains how to read its diagram, including that the rollback boxes are not flag values and that the flag keeps its old value until the final step. Its failure cases say exactly what happens, so a newcomer can follow the flow, where state lives and what happens on failure with less doubt. B is less clear because it sets the flag partway through rollback and its failure notes contradict themselves (it says "no partial rollback starts" even though the freeze has already happened).

author: sonnet
reason: Document A is easier to follow: it defines its terms first and shows rollback as one ordered sequence (freeze, drain, reconcile, reprocess, hand off, flip), with one stalled state for failures. Document B covers the same ground with more detail, but its diagram is crowded with retry self-loops, it sends the reader to other sections, and some sentences are harder to parse, such as rule 2 with its exception.

author: sonnet
reason: A states each step's trigger, outcomes, failure handling and state location more explicitly and consistently, for example how workers pause charging during a rollback while the flag stays unchanged, and the separate one-action rollback from shadow; B leaves gaps, such as freezing the old engine during a shadow rollback and not explaining how handoff charging is enabled before the flip.

author: haiku
reason: B is easier to follow: it names the four possible outcomes first, gives a clean diagram with numbered nodes, has a table showing what state each service stores, and its failure table shows the effect on cart, money and stock, while A covers the same flow with more repetition and a more tangled flowchart.

author: haiku
reason: Document A is quicker to understand and harder to misread: it names the four possible endings up front, follows with a short numbered flow and a clean diagram with labelled steps, and has tables showing where each service's state lives and what happens to cart, money and stock in each failure, whereas Document B's flowchart is more tangled (both claim results feed back into a second decision) and B never collects stored state in one place.

author: sonnet
reason: A explains the flow in a short plain-language summary, makes the stock-reservation call a simple synchronous reply, and gives each step its trigger, its action, where the data is stored and what happens on failure; B mixes HTTP requests that get event replies and splits its reading conventions across several places, which takes more effort to follow, though its order-status list is useful.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A opens with a one-sentence summary and a key to the diagram, puts each service's tables and the customer's view inside the diagram, labels every arrow with what triggers it, and adds an order-status tree, so a newcomer can follow the triggers, state and failure branches more quickly; Document B is clean too, but it mixes processed_events with processed_webhooks and reuses its dotted 'event' arrow style for a timer, which leaves small ambiguities.

author: haiku
reason: A is easier to follow: it opens with a one-paragraph summary of the whole design and gives a state table showing who holds each row and what state comes next. It traces one notification through seven numbered steps and lists every failure with its outcome in a single table. B's ownership model is sound, but the reader has to piece it together from dense invariants and a long, SQL-heavy step 3, with no overview and no end-to-end flow.

author: haiku
reason: B is faster to understand: it opens with a plain summary of how the system works today and after the change, gives one state table for the row, walks through a single notification in seven numbered steps, and puts all failures in one table, while A makes the reader track a separate owner field alongside status, plus dense invariants and an ambiguity rule, before the flow becomes clear.

author: sonnet
reason: Document A explains the runtime on its own: a four-step flow overview, a table of where state lives, numbered steps that each say what triggers them and what happens on a crash, and a single failure table, all kept apart from the rollout plan. Document B spreads the same mechanics across a long list of shipping steps, so the reader has to piece the runtime together from steps 3 and 4.

author: sonnet
reason: B describes how the system runs as one numbered sequence (record, pick the path, hand off, store, send, report back, reconcile), with a state-ownership table and a failure table, and keeps the rollout plan separate, whereas A spreads the runtime mechanism across long, repetitive shipping steps.
